subject: Law
title: 3. Establishment and Jurisdiction of Civil Courts

segments.text: Civil courts decide private-law disputes such as property, contracts, declarations, injunctions and other civil rights, subject to statutory jurisdiction.

The topic is about the hierarchy of civil courts and the difference between a court hearing a matter first and a court reviewing a lower court decision. Jurisdiction may depend on subject matter, territory, pecuniary limits and statutory allocation.

A civil court cannot decide a dispute merely because the parties prefer that forum. It must possess jurisdiction conferred by law. Jurisdiction answers whether a court has legal competence over the type of controversy, the geographical connection, the monetary value where pecuniary limits apply, and the level of adjudication at which the matter is brought.

The hierarchy of civil courts is therefore only one part of the topic. The more fundamental question is allocation of judicial authority. A special statute may create a specialized tribunal or exclusive forum and thereby alter the normal route through the ordinary civil courts.

Subject-matter jurisdiction concerns the legal nature of the dispute: for example, an ordinary civil claim, a family matter, a revenue dispute or a matter assigned by statute to a special forum. Territorial jurisdiction concerns the geographical link between the dispute and the court. Pecuniary jurisdiction concerns monetary thresholds where the relevant law uses them. Personal jurisdiction concerns legal authority over the parties where that question is relevant.

Original jurisdiction means that the court is the first judicial forum to determine the case. Appellate jurisdiction exists only where the law creates a right of appeal and specifies the appellate forum. Revision, review and constitutional supervisory jurisdiction are different remedies and should not be described as if they were ordinary appeals.

For a jurisdiction problem, ask four questions in order: What is the legal nature of the claim? Is any statute excluding or specially assigning jurisdiction? Which territorial facts connect the dispute to a court? If pecuniary allocation applies, which court is competent by value? Only after these questions should the answer move to the hierarchy of appeal.

A jurisdictional objection can be decisive because a judgment delivered without the legally required competence may be vulnerable even if the judge’s reasoning on the underlying dispute appears persuasive.

items.text: Jurisdiction means legal authority to hear and decide a matter. Before discussing court hierarchy, first identify why a particular court is legally competent to take the case.
Original jurisdiction means the case starts before that court. Appellate jurisdiction means the court examines a decision of a lower court because the law gives a right of appeal.

Territorial jurisdiction asks where the cause, property or parties connect with the court's area. Pecuniary jurisdiction concerns monetary limits. Subject-matter jurisdiction concerns the legal nature of the dispute.
When solving a problem, ask in order:
Is it a civil matter? Which territorial area is connected? Is there any monetary limit? Has a special statute given the matter to a special forum?

rows: Common confusion to avoid: Do not use “jurisdiction” as a synonym for “power” in a vague sense. In procedural law it is a legal competence that must exist before valid adjudication.

items.text: Learn the meaning of jurisdiction before learning court names.
Prepare original vs appellate jurisdiction with examples.
Understand territorial, pecuniary and subject-matter jurisdiction.
Use the applicable civil-courts law/bare act for exact institutional details.

segments.text: Original jurisdiction = first hearing of the suit.
Appellate jurisdiction = review of a lower court judgment/order where appeal is provided.
A court must have lawful jurisdiction before deciding a case.
Jurisdiction can depend on territory, value and nature of dispute.
